summary: Compare the top SaaS onboarding automation platforms in 2026. Learn which tools provision accounts without SCIM for growing companies.
body_markdown:
At a growing company, setting up SaaS accounts for one new hire by hand takes[about 1.5 hours](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/state-of-saas-access-management-2026) .[SaaS onboarding automation](https://www.accessowl.com/use-cases/automate-onboarding-offboarding) platforms claim to eliminate that work, but most of them assume every app in your stack supports SCIM provisioning. When half your tools are on standard plans without those enterprise features, your automated workflow becomes a fancy to-do list that still requires manual work for each app.


## TL;DR


-


**Best overall for growing companies:** AccessOwl. It creates accounts in 500+ SaaS apps[without SCIM](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/what-is-scim-provisioning) , triggered from your HRIS. HR and Operations managers can run it, not only IT.


-


**How SaaS onboarding automation works:** Your HRIS or IdP flags a start date. An access template picks the apps by role or department. The tool then creates each account and gives employees an easy way to request access to other apps.


-


**What these tools replace:** AccessOwl's State of SaaS Access Management 2026 found that a new hire at the median company needs 9 apps, held by 5 different app admins. Setting that up by hand takes[about 1.5 hours](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/state-of-saas-access-management-2026) .


-


**What to check before you buy:** Whether the tool creates accounts in apps without SCIM. SCIM usually needs an Enterprise plan in each app.


-


**Also compared:** YeshID (small teams, free under 20 users), Deel IT (an HR platform with an IT add-on) and Lumos (enterprise identity governance).


## What Is SaaS Onboarding Automation


Every time a new employee joins your company, someone on your team has to set up accounts across a dozen or more SaaS applications. When you're the sole IT hire at a company that is rapidly hiring, that process can eat hours out of your week.


SaaS onboarding automation uses software to automatically provision user accounts, assign permissions, and configure access across your organization's SaaS stack whenever a new hire starts. Instead of manually creating each account and chasing down tool owners, an automated system handles the work based on predefined templates tied to roles, teams, or departments.


### What Manual Onboarding Actually Looks Like


Without automation, HR notifies IT late, IT creates accounts one by one across 10 to 20 apps, permissions get assigned inconsistently, and new employees sit idle on day one. Each access request can take 30 minutes or more when you factor in back-and-forth messages and manual account creation.


An IT manager at an eye care marketing company told us how onboarding worked before they automated it:


> "We used to have a spreadsheet, and people would ask me to add someone to Google Workspace. Then a week later they'd ask why that person wasn't in the office group, and I'd reply 'well, nobody told me'."


Automated provisioning ties directly into compliance frameworks such as SOC 2, ISO 27001, and HIPAA, which require audit trails showing who was granted access, when, and by whom. It also handles offboarding. Orphaned accounts left by departing employees are among the most common security gaps at growing companies.


## Buyer Criteria for SaaS Onboarding Automation Tools


We aggregated data from conversations with[115 companies](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/saas-onboarding-automation-platforms#:~:text=Methodology%20of%20the%20Buyer%20Criteria%20Data) that assessed multiple solutions to automate SaaS onboarding. These five criteria came up most often:


**New hire in, accounts created:** Buyers want onboarding to end with a real account in each app, not a ticket or a Slack reminder to an app owner. A tool that sends a task to an app owner without actually creating an account scored lower. We checked whether each tool creates the account itself or hands the work back to IT.


**Coverage beyond SCIM and Enterprise plans:** Most stacks have apps the identity provider can't reach. Some apps have no SCIM or admin API. Others keep SCIM behind an Enterprise tier. Many growing companies don't have enterprise tier subscriptions for every app in their stack, so a tool that only works through those protocols has a serious blind spot. We counted how many apps each tool can create accounts in without SCIM.


**Onboarding starts from the HRIS:** A new hire added in BambooHR, HiBob, Personio, Rippling or Deel should start onboarding on their start date, with no ticket to IT. Many buyers test their own HR system during the trial before they commit. We checked which HR systems each tool connects to and whether the start date triggers onboarding.


**The right apps for each role, picked automatically:** A common best practice is to use access templates based on role, department and location. Buyers want the HRIS fields to pick the template, so nobody chooses apps by hand.


**Ready on day one, with an easy way to ask for more:** Buyers want every tool working on the new hire's first morning, not days later. Anything outside the template should be one request away, with multi-step approval chains you can set per application. We checked how new hires request extra apps and how approvals are routed.

## Deel IT


Most teams have an HRIS long before they have dedicated IT software, so a natural next step is to look at the IT add-on from their current HR tool. Deel IT is one example of an HR tool that offers IT on top: laptops, device security and app access, all from the employee record HR already created. Rippling IT is another popular option. All of them share the same limitations, because app access still runs through your identity provider.


### What It Is


Deel IT adds devices, IT support and access management on top of Deel HR. For app access, Deel says it isn't an identity provider. It syncs with the one you already use, such as Microsoft Entra, Google Workspace, Okta or JumpCloud. Deel decides who should get what from HR data, and your IdP creates the accounts.


### What It Covers for IT Provisioning


-


**Access Groups:** Groups built from role, team or location map to a set of apps. A new designer added in Deel can get Slack, Figma and Notion in one go.


-


**Devices for new hires:** Deel IT can order, set up and ship laptops. Equipment and app access start from the same record.


-


**Approval workflows:** Deel's workflow builder can add approval steps before access is granted.


For a deeper look at how HR platforms handle IT provisioning, see our guide to[automating SaaS provisioning with Deel](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/deel-hris-tools-to-automate-saas-provisioning) .


### Limitations


-


**App coverage depends on your IdP:** New hires only get automatic accounts in apps your IdP can provision. Google Workspace automates provisioning for about 57 apps, and Deel doesn't publish its own list. The rest are set up by hand.


-


**SCIM is often an Enterprise feature:** The apps your IdP can provision usually need SCIM, which many vendors keep for their Enterprise plans.


-


**Per-group app choice needs an "enhanced" IdP:** Deel's FAQ says choosing apps per group only works where Deel has an "enhanced" integration, such as Google and JumpCloud.


-


**Roles inside each app stay manual:** Deel creates the account but doesn't set the role or permission level inside each app.


-


**Price:** Access Management is only on Deel IT's top plan. Deel's pricing page lists Deel IT Scale at $149 per user per month, bundled with device management, endpoint protection and 24/7 IT support. AccessOwl's pricing is public and starts at $250 a month.


If your team already runs Deel, AccessOwl works alongside it. It's on the[Deel Marketplace](https://marketplace.deel.wtf/en/apps/access-owl) , connects to 50+ other HR systems and syncs with your IdP. New hires get the same HR-driven setup, with accounts in more apps and the right role in each one.


## YeshID


YeshID markets itself as an AI-native identity and access control solution built around lifecycle automation, role-based access control, Shadow IT visibility, and a freemium tier for small teams. If you're running a team of fewer than 20 people and want to get started with some form of identity management without spending anything upfront, it's worth a look.


### What YeshID Offers


-


An AI agent called Rae that assists with policy workflows and integration setup through conversational interactions


-


Lifecycle automation across HRIS systems, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Okta. Starting onboarding from your HRIS and connecting Okta need the Business plan, which has custom pricing.


-


Access requests through Slack or Microsoft Teams with configurable approval workflows


-


A free tier for teams under 20 users, with paid plans from $9 per user per month, billed annually


The AI agent Rae is designed to help you set up policies conversationally. In practice, though, the AI layer introduces abstraction where you want deterministic, repeatable workflows. When provisioning accounts or revoking access, you need to know exactly what's going to happen every time.


YeshID's docs list 158 apps, and 140 of them support provisioning. Each one connects through SCIM or a REST API, and the docs note that capabilities can depend on the app's own plan. For apps outside that list, new hires get their accounts by hand.


### Where It Fits


YeshID works best for very small teams, think under 20 employees, that want a free or low cost entry point into identity management.


### Where It Falls Short


The gap between feature list and real world maturity becomes noticeable as your company grows. If you're scaling past 50 employees and need reliable, hands off automated provisioning across a diverse SaaS stack, you'll likely hit limits. YeshID is a reasonable place to experiment, but it's not where most IT teams will want to stay long term.


## Cakewalk


Cakewalk positions itself as identity governance with a clean, polished interface. Its product pages advertise over 5,600 supported apps, and it offers customizable workflows plus a browser extension that maps the apps employees use. On the surface, that's a compelling package. But the details matter when you're deciding what will actually reduce your workload versus what just reorganizes it.


### What Cakewalk Offers


-


App and AI agent discovery across SaaS environments, giving you visibility into what tools employees are actually using and where shadow IT might be hiding


-


Customizable approval workflows and a policy builder for defining access rules, so you can map out multi-step approval chains that match your org structure


-


Automated provisioning for 75 apps, 16 through a vendor API key and 59 through Agent Cake, which works in each app's admin console the way a person would


-


An open API for building custom integrations when their native connectors don't cover your stack


### Where It Fits


If your primary pain point is messy approval workflows and you want a clean interface, Cakewalk delivers. For teams that already have provisioning handled through Okta and mainly need a governance layer on top, it could fill that gap.


### Where It Falls Short


Cakewalk offers integrations that don't require SCIM, but the catalog is small. Its integration guides list 75 apps with automated provisioning, compared to the 5,600+ supported apps on its product pages. Auto-provisioning only arrived in March 2025. For every other app, a new hire's account is still a task for someone to complete.


### Bottom Line


Cakewalk makes access management look good. The interface is sharp, the workflow builder is flexible, and discovery coverage is broad. But if what you need is a tool that provisions and deprovisions accounts on your behalf without requiring you to build custom integrations for each app, you'll find that the automation depth isn't there yet. For IT managers who need onboarding software that handles the underlying account creation and removal directly, the gap between governance visibility and true automated provisioning is worth weighing carefully before committing.


## Lumos


Lumos positions itself as an autonomous identity governance solution, and it's one of the more ambitious products in this space. The tool gives IT and security teams visibility and control over identities across all applications, with the company reporting that its average enterprise customer manages around 650 apps through the product. That number alone tells you something about where Lumos is aimed. Lumos says it's built for mid-market and enterprise teams, "generally 200+ employees." For a detailed comparison, see our[Lumos vs AccessOwl head-to-head](https://www.accessowl.com/alternatives/lumos-vs-accessowl) .


### What Lumos Offers


-


Autonomous policy management powered by an AI agent called Albus, which handles policy creation and enforcement across your identity stack


-


Full lifecycle automation for joiner, mover, and leaver workflows, covering onboarding, role changes, and offboarding in a single system


-


SaaS spend management with license optimization, so you can identify unused seats and reclaim wasted budget alongside your access governance


-


Access reviews with AI powered risk detection, flagging anomalous access patterns instead of treating every review as a flat checklist


-


Several ways to connect apps: SCIM connectors, direct API connectors, an on-premises agent and, since early 2026, browser agents. Its catalog lists 101 SaaS apps but doesn't say which method each one uses


The spend management angle is a notable addition. Most tools in this category focus purely on access, but Lumos bundles in license tracking and cost optimization. If your CFO is asking why you're paying for 200 Figma seats when only 80 people logged in last quarter, that feature alone might catch your attention.


### Where It Fits


Lumos is built for larger enterprises with hundreds of applications and dedicated security teams. If your organization has a full-time security function, a complex identity stack spanning cloud and on-premise environments, and the budget for a premium governance solution, Lumos delivers serious depth. The company says it deploys 7x faster than legacy IGA tools while costing 80 percent less than those same legacy options, making it competitive in the enterprise IGA market.


### Where It Falls Short


That enterprise positioning is exactly what makes Lumos a tough fit for most Series A through Series C companies. When you're a solo IT hire managing 30 to 80 apps (not 650), you need something opinionated and fast, not a governance engine designed for complex multi-team security organizations. The feature set assumes you have the headcount and processes to take advantage of autonomous policy management and AI-driven risk scoring, and if you don't, much of that capability sits unused.


Pricing also reflects the enterprise target audience. Lumos doesn't publish prices, but its own AWS Marketplace listing prices the core platform at $27,000 for a 12-month contract, plus $180 a year for each additional user. While Lumos is cheaper than legacy IGA vendors like SailPoint or Saviynt, "cheaper than legacy IGA" and "affordable for a 100-person startup" are very different benchmarks.


### Bottom Line


Lumos is a strong choice if you're operating at enterprise scale with a security team that needs autonomous governance across hundreds of apps. But if you're at a growing company where speed of deployment and straightforward automated provisioning matter more than AI driven policy engines, it's built for a different stage of growth than where you are right now.

## Methodology of the Buyer Criteria Data


The buyer criteria in this article come from conversations with 115 companies that evaluated onboarding automation tools. About two-thirds were SaaS, FinTech or HealthTech companies, and almost all were companies under 1,000 employees. IT managers were the most common buyer, followed by engineering leads, and HR & Ops managers.


## FAQs


### How do I automate onboarding across all our SaaS apps?


Start from your HR system. When HR adds a new hire, SaaS provisioning tools like AccessOwl read their department, role and start date. They pick the apps the person needs from an access template and create each account on the start date.


Check the last step before you buy. Many tools only create accounts in apps that support SCIM, and SCIM usually needs an Enterprise plan in each app. AccessOwl creates accounts in 500+ SaaS apps through integration accounts, with no SCIM needed.


### Does my HR system create app accounts for new hires on its own?


Usually not. HR systems like BambooHR, HiBob, Personio or CharlieHR hold the start date, role and manager. They don't create accounts in apps like Slack, Figma or GitHub.


Some HR platforms sell an IT add-on, such as Deel IT. These add-ons create accounts through your identity provider, so they only reach the apps your IdP can provision. AccessOwl connects to your HR system and creates the accounts in each app when HR adds a new hire.


### How do I give new hires the right apps for their role?


Use access templates. A template bundles the apps and permissions one group needs, set by department, role, location or employment type. Templates stack. Everyone can get Slack and Google Workspace, and Sales also gets Salesforce.


In AccessOwl, the new hire's HR data picks the templates, and each template sets the role inside the app too, like an Editor seat in Figma. You can preview which apps someone will get before their first day.


### I work in HR or Operations and IT landed on my plate. Can I automate onboarding without an IT team?


Yes. Look for a tool a non-technical person can set up and run. With AccessOwl, HR adds the new hire in the HR system as usual. AccessOwl applies the matching templates and creates the accounts on the start date. Managers can add or approve apps in Slack.


Connecting an app means inviting an integration account, so there are no scripts to write. AccessOwl is built for companies of 30 to 1,000 people that don't want a full identity suite like Okta.


### Can Okta or Google Workspace create accounts in every app for new hires?


No. Okta, Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID only create accounts in apps they have a provisioning connection for. For most apps that connection is SCIM, which many vendors keep for their Enterprise plan. Every other app still needs someone to create the account by hand.


AccessOwl works alongside your identity provider. It adds people to the Okta, Google or Entra groups you already use, and it creates accounts directly in the apps your IdP can't reach.


### Can one tool handle both onboarding and offboarding?


Yes. With one tool, the list of apps a new hire got on day one is the same list that gets cleaned up when they leave. AccessOwl creates the accounts when someone starts and removes their access in each app on their last working day, both triggered from your HR system.


For a comparison of offboarding tools, see our guide to the[best offboarding automation tools](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/best-tools-automating-offboarding-access-revocation) .


### How do I choose the right SaaS onboarding automation tool for my company's size?


Focus on whether the tool can provision accounts without requiring SCIM or SAML support, since most Series A through Series C companies don't have enterprise-tier subscriptions across their entire stack. Look for deployment speed measured in days instead of weeks, and check if the tool handles both onboarding and offboarding automatically without requiring a dedicated identity governance team.


### Which onboarding automation tool works best for solo IT hires?


AccessOwl and YeshID are both designed for smaller IT teams, but they differ in the depth of their provisioning. AccessOwl provisions accounts directly across apps without SCIM requirements using API integrations and RPA, while YeshID's free tier works for teams under 20 people but may require more manual configuration as you scale past 50 employees.


### What's the difference between governance tools and true provisioning automation?


Governance tools like Cakewalk give you visibility into who has access and let you build approval workflows, but they often don't automatically create or remove accounts. True provisioning automation means the system actually creates user accounts, sets permissions, and revokes access without requiring manual work from IT or tool owners for each request.


### When should I consider an enterprise-focused solution like Lumos?


If you're managing over 200 apps with a dedicated security team and need autonomous policy management across complex identity environments, enterprise solutions make sense. But if you're a solo IT hire at a company with 50 to 150 employees managing 30 to 80 apps, tools built for enterprise scale will create implementation overhead without delivering proportional value at your current stage.


### Can onboarding automation tools handle apps that don't support SCIM or SAML?


Most tools in this category require SCIM or SAML, so any app that doesn't support those protocols becomes a manual task. AccessOwl is the exception, using direct API connections, RPA, and browser automation to provision accounts even when vendors don't offer enterprise identity protocols, which matters when you're not paying for top-tier plans across your entire SaaS stack.
